text: François de Malherbe (1555–16 October 1628) was a French poet, critic, and translator. Born in Le Locheur (near Caen, Normandie), he came from a family of standing, though its noble lineage did not meet the heraldic standards for pre-16th century nobility. He was the eldest son of François de Malherbe, a conseiller du roi in Caen’s magistracy. Malherbe received an elaborate education in Caen, Paris, Heidelberg, and Basel. At twenty-one, he entered the household of Henri d'Angoulême, the illegitimate son of Henry II and governor of Provence, serving as secretary and marrying there in 1581. According to Tallemant des Réaux, his early verses were of poor quality. After Henri d'Angoulême died during Malherbe’s visit to Provence, he had no steady employment, though he earned a significant sum from Henry III through servile verses, which he later libelled. For many years, he lived between Provence and Normandy, with little known about this period. His work *Larmes de Saint Pierre*, imitated from Luigi Tansillo, was published in 1587. In 1600, he composed an ode of welcome for Maria de' Medici, marking the first of his notable poems. It took several years for his fortunes to improve; he was introduced to Henry IV by Cardinal Du Perron, though the king initially showed little interest, eventually summoning him to court and providing him with support, though the promised pension was not paid until after Henry IV’s reign. His father died in 1606, and Malherbe inherited his estate. From then on, he lived at court, maintaining a close correspondence with his wife, though seeing her only twice in twenty years. In old age, he suffered a major tragedy when his son, Marc Antoine, died in a duel against Paul de Fortia de Piles. Malherbe suspected foul play and used his influence to have de Fortia and Jean Baptiste de Covet brought to justice; he died before the case was resolved, reportedly from disease contracted during the siege of La Rochelle, where he had gone to petition the king. He died in Paris on 16 October 1628, at the age of seventy-three, just 15 months after his son’s death. The football team from Caen, France, Stade Malherbe de Caen, founded in 1913, is named after him. Malherbe had a significant and lasting impact on French literature, particularly in establishing the poetic rules of "Classicism" that would dominate for nearly two centuries until the Romantic era. His emphasis on technical perfection, simplicity, and vocabulary purity offered a corrective to the excesses of Pierre de Ronsard and La Pléiade, though Boileau-Despréaux’s praise in "Enfin Malherbe vint" is limited by his lack of knowledge of earlier French poetry. Malherbe’s personal character, marked by a bludgeon-like wit, was not amiable, as noted by his contemporary and rival Mathurin Régnier, who opposed him not only for his loyalty to Ronsard but also due to Malherbe’s discourtesy toward Régnier’s uncle, Philippe Desportes, whom Malherbe had initially plagiarized. While his poetic output is limited and often frigid, his best-known works include the *Consolation a Duperier* (featuring the line “Et, rose, elle a vécu ce que vivent les roses”), his odes to Marie de' Medici and Louis XIII. His prose is more extensive and highly refined, including translations of Livy and Seneca and numerous well-written letters, many addressed to Peiresc, as well as a detailed and critical commentary on Desportes. His most important disciples were François Maynard and Racan; Claude Favre de Vaugelas is credited with purifying French diction around the same time. Two of his poems were set to music by Maurice Jaubert. The primary biographical sources are Racan’s *Vie de Malherbe* and Tallemant des Réaux’s *Historiette*. The standard edition of his works is *Oeuvres poétiques*, edited by René Fromilhague and Raymond Lebègue (1968), while Antoine Adam’s popular collection *Poésies* is based on the Pléiade edition (1982). Key secondary sources include G. Brunot’s *La Doctrine de Malherbe* (1891), René Fromilhague’s *Malherbe: Technique et création poétique* (1954), David Lee Rubin’s *High Hidden Order* (1972) and its appendix in *The Knot of Artifice* (1981), and Claude K. Abraham’s *Enfin Malherbe* (1971), which focuses on Malherbe’s prosody.
